extracted.intended_audience: historians and scholars of the history of mathematics; editors and authors of a multi-volume cultural history; academic researchers in history, philosophy, and mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and thematic structure for a six-volume, global cultural history of mathematics (antiquity to the modern age), aimed at editors and chapter authors; outlines recurring chapter themes, editorial selection principles, and methodological emphases. Serves as an organiser's report and chapter abstract collection for the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven general themes (volume structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each volume addresses seven general themes in as many chapters: Everyday Numeracy; Practice and Profession; Inventing Mathematics; Mathematics and Worldviews; Describing and Understanding the World; Mathematics and Technological Change; Representing Mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These seven thematic chapters provide the overall structure for the six-volume project; each volume begins with the first three (Everyday Numeracy, Practice and Profession, Inventing Mathematics), follows with the three about larger impacts (Mathematics and Worldviews, Describing and Understanding the World, Mathematics and Technological Change), and ends with Representing Mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between representative features and long-term significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume editors must confront difficult choices about which topics and cultures to include and should try to strike a balance between representative features of the period and particular developments of long-term significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should weigh breadth (representative features) against highlighting developments that had lasting impact when selecting topics and authors for chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special emphasis on material culture and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: All six volumes place special emphasis on the material culture of mathematical activities and on how mathematical knowledge changed over time alongside new forms of communication and circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters should consider artifacts, tools, and media of transmission (texts, diagrams, instruments) and trace changes in circulation and communication as central elements of mathematical practice and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a cultural view of mathematics (begin with indefiniteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cultural view begins with the indefiniteness of what 'mathematics' meant in different times and places and takes seriously that definitions and boundaries shifted historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historiography and epistemological questions should be foregrounded: avoid imposing a single modern definition of mathematics; treat the category as historically constituted and variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present concrete aspects in new, informative, and eye-opening ways
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief aim: to present concrete aspects of mathematics in ancient (and other) times in ways that will be new, informative, and eye opening for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should aim for fresh interpretations, accessible presentation of evidence, and insights that challenge common assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat numeracy as a culturally conditioned spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeracy is conceived as a spectrum of abilities (from estimating size to performing complicated calculations) that is culturally conditioned by practices, beliefs, tools, and artifacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters on Everyday Numeracy should analyze a range of practices among non-professionals and professionals, consider tools and artifacts, and be cautious about rigidly separating 'general public' and 'professionals'. Use historical texts and artifacts to map the spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze varied milieus and professions of mathematical practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practitioners come from diverse milieus; methods and uses of mathematics vary by profession and social context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify types of texts (problems, procedural texts, tables), connect them to historical context, discuss modes of schooling and transmission (schools, private masters, familial transmission), and assess social role and status even when documents are unsigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when attributing 'invention' or originality in ancient contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: For cuneiform cultures it is often arbitrary to decide that a text contains a specific invention; in Greek contexts authorship and originality were socially promoted, making 'invention' a more applicable metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anachronistic claims of invention; distinguish culturally specific practices of authorship, transmission, and novelty when identifying innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume axiomatic-deductive demonstration as universal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiomatic-deductive demonstration was decisive in Greek mathematics but was not a necessary condition for sophisticated mathematics in other cultures (Egypt, Mesopotamia, India, China).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare different traditions on their own terms; recognize a variety of valid mathematical modes (algorithmic, procedural, empirical, geometric) and avoid privileging the Greek deductive model as the universal norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address fundamental questions about mathematics' objects, branches, cognition, explanatory power, and moral implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters should consider: (1) what mathematics studies and whether there are separate mathematical objects; (2) relations among branches (arithmetic, geometry, applied studies); (3) what modes of cognition mathematics secures and the applicability of deductive demonstration; (4) how mathematics contributes to understanding natural phenomena and its limits; (5) moral/religious implications and the relation of training in mathematics to fulfillment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list of interrelated issues to frame discussions of how mathematics functioned within world-views and intellectual life in each period and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine mathematical modeling and cross-cultural transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Study how mathematical methods (e.g., Babylonian linear methods, sexagesimal notation) were adapted and transformed across cultures (e.g., imported and adapted in the Hellenistic period), and how different traditions emphasized different modelling goals (Babylonian synodic moments vs Greek predictive positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace concrete technical transmissions (notations, algorithms, computational frameworks) and how they were integrated with indigenous mathematical styles (geometry, trigonometry, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing the modern 'applied science' dichotomy on ancient technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not uncritically adopt the modern epistemic claim that technology is merely the handmaiden of science; the head/hand (epistēmē/technē) divide is historically specific and may mislead interpretations of ancient practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate technology and mathematical knowledge as potentially intertwined forms of expertise; reconstruct craft practices and somatic know-how alongside abstract textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze representations of mathematics in word and image across genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Study ancient verbal and visual depictions of mathematics and mathematicians (practical, theoretical, recreational) and how branch-terms carried non-mathematical meanings that shaped representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider portrayals in literature, drama, biographies, and non-mathematical texts; note that many representations are produced by non-mathematicians and can reveal cultural attitudes toward mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for global and literate-tradition balance (CSAPGL focus with scope remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume II and the project more broadly aim to offer a culturally balanced view of global mathematics, focusing on surviving literate traditions preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian, Greek, and Latin (CSAPGL), while briefly surveying traces from other regions acknowledging scope limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include CSAPGL traditions in depth but acknowledge and indicate research needs for underrepresented regions; be explicit about scope and limits of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent thematic application across periods while allowing period-specific character
rubrics_metrics.description: Although each volume has its own distinctive character, the seven overarching themes recur in every volume to provide continuity, while editors and chapter authors tailor treatments to period-specific concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the seven themes consistently as an organising principle, but let editors emphasize period-appropriate methodologies, sources, and emphases in introductory essays and chapters.
